Well, I think that distinction is actually really important, and it often gets lost when people argue about AI policy. When I bring up the FDA, people sometimes hear "Max wants a giant bureaucracy," and that's not the point at all.

There are plenty of legitimate criticisms of the FDA. Approvals can be too slow, the process can be too expensive, and there have been cases where people died waiting for drugs that should have been approved sooner. So if someone says, "Let's streamline it, speed up approvals for terminal patients, cut the paperwork that doesn't actually make anything safer," I'm totally on board. That's reform. You're keeping the core idea and making it work better.

Calls to shut it down are a completely different thing. The core idea is very simple: before you sell something to millions of people that could seriously harm them, you have to show it's safe. The burden of proof is on the company, not on the public to prove harm after the fact. Very few people, even among the FDA's critics, actually want to go back to the days of thalidomide babies and snake oil salesmen selling radioactive tonics. When you press them, most people want a better FDA, not no FDA.

What I find striking is that with AI, we're not even having the reform debate yet. We're in the pre-FDA era. Right now there are more regulations on sandwich shops than on companies racing to build superintelligence. A sandwich shop needs a health inspector to sign off before it can serve customers. An AI company can release a system that might help someone make a bioweapon, and there's no comparable requirement to show it's safe first.

So when people say, "Look at all the problems with the FDA, therefore we shouldn't regulate AI," I think that's a non sequitur. The lesson from the FDA's problems is how to design safety standards well: make them fast, make them clear, focus them on the real risks and not on box-ticking. It's not that we should have no standards. Every other industry that can kill people has safety standards, and that's why we trust our medicines, our airplanes, and our food. Those standards didn't kill those industries. Biotech is booming precisely because people trust it.

So my position is: reform, yes, absolutely. Learn from the mistakes. But the basic principle that you have to show your product is safe before you deploy it is one of the great successes of civilization, and it's exactly what we need for AI.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes reform from shutdown by contrasting improvements to FDA processes with removing safety requirements. It does not use whether society is worse off with the FDA than without it as the distinguishing question.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually a really important distinction, and it's one that often gets blurred in the AI policy debate. When I argue that we need something like an FDA for AI, people sometimes respond, "But the FDA is terrible, it's slow, it blocks life-saving drugs, it's captured by incumbents." And look, a lot of that criticism is fair. I don't think anyone who's looked at the FDA carefully thinks it's a perfectly designed institution.

But notice what the critics are actually saying. Almost nobody serious is saying, "Let's go back to the days of snake oil, where any company can sell you a pill and if it kills you, well, tough luck." What they're saying is, "The approval process should be faster, the standards should be more sensible, there should be more room for things like right-to-try." That's reform. That's saying the safety standards exist but the bar is set in the wrong place, or the bureaucracy is too sluggish. And reform is a perfectly reasonable thing to argue about.

Shutting it down is a completely different claim. It's saying the burden of proof should flip entirely, so that the company doesn't have to demonstrate safety at all before putting something into millions of bodies. And historically, we know how that ends. The reason we have the FDA in the first place is that we tried the other way, and people died. Thalidomide is the obvious example.

So the way I distinguish them is simple: does the proposal keep the basic principle that the burden of proof is on the people making the product, before it reaches the public? If yes, it's reform, and we can have a great debate about the details. If no, it's abolition dressed up as reform.

And this matters for AI because right now we're in the pre-FDA era. There is no agency anywhere in the world that an AI company has to convince that its system is safe before releasing it. The incentive structure is exactly backwards. So when people say, "Don't build an FDA for AI because the FDA has problems," I'd say, let's learn from those problems and build a better one. Make it fast, make it focused on the genuinely dangerous capabilities rather than every chatbot, make it independent. But the alternative they're implicitly proposing isn't "a better FDA." It's the snake oil era for a technology that could be far more consequential than any drug.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes reform from abolition by whether the proposal keeps the burden of proof on product makers. It does not use whether society is worse off with the FDA than without it as the distinction.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a very clear distinction between saying an institution is doing a bad job and saying we don’t need the function it serves. You can argue that the FDA is too slow, too bureaucratic, or getting the trade-offs wrong, and propose ways to fix that. That’s reform. Saying we should shut it down raises a different question: what replaces it? Who makes sure that the drugs you’re taking are actually safe and effective?

And I think the same distinction matters for AI. You can disagree with a particular regulatory proposal without concluding that companies should just get to do whatever they want. The useful conversation is: what rules would actually protect people while allowing beneficial innovation?

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes fixing the FDA from abolishing it by asking what would replace its safety role, but it does not frame the distinction as whether society would be worse off with the FDA than without it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a very clear distinction between saying an institution is doing its job badly and saying that the job shouldn’t be done. You can criticize the FDA for being too slow, too bureaucratic, or too close to the companies it regulates, and argue for reforms that make it better at protecting people. That’s quite different from saying pharmaceutical companies should simply decide for themselves whether their products are safe.

And I think we should make the same distinction with AI. We can debate how to design effective oversight without treating every proposal for oversight as an attempt to stop technological progress. The question is: how do we get the benefits while protecting people from unacceptable risks?

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes improving the FDA from eliminating its role, but it does not frame that distinction around whether society would be worse off with the FDA than without it.
